crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers the conversion of recorded speech into written text and the labelling of who said what in a multi person conversation. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where the transcript is the working document that later coding, memoing and theme building depend on. The scope runs from a single research interview to focus groups, panel discussions and fieldwork recordings with overlapping talk. It also covers the alignment of transcript timestamps to the audio so a reader can return to the moment a claim was made.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on audio capture, usually a phone, a portable recorder or a conferencing platform, and on a compute layer that performs speech recognition and speaker diarization. Diarization models segment the audio by voice and assign each segment to a speaker, while automatic speech recognition produces the words. Cloud services and local models are both common, and the choice usually turns on recording length, accent coverage, language and whether the audio may leave the institution. Storage and backup of the original audio matter as much as the transcript file itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline cleans the audio, runs diarization, runs recognition, then merges the two outputs into a speaker labelled transcript. Researchers then correct names, technical terms and overlaps by hand, because error rates rise with crosstalk, poor microphones and strong accents. Many teams keep a two pass routine, an automatic first draft followed by a full listen through against the audio. Some also keep a verbatim version and a cleaned version, since the level of detail needed for conversation analysis differs from that needed for thematic coding.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Transcripts are identifiable data even when names are removed, because voices, workplaces and personal stories can re identify a participant. Consent forms and ethics approvals therefore need to state whether audio will be sent to a third party service, where it is processed and how long it is retained. Provenance matters too, so a transcript should record the tool, the model version, the date and the human edits applied. On this site, content links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which keeps the chain from claim back to source intact.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Accuracy on clean single speaker audio is now good enough that most effort has moved to the hard cases, overlapping speech, code switching, domain vocabulary and low resource languages. Diarization is improving on short turns and on recordings with many speakers, and on device processing is becoming more practical as models shrink. The open questions are less about raw word error rate and more about how much human correction a study can afford and how transparently that correction is reported. Expect tighter integration between transcription tools and the coding software that qualitative researchers already use.
